extracted.intended_audience: 19th-century Republican voters and the general public (mid-19th-century American electorate); readers of an anti-slavery political address
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-19th-century political address arguing against slavery and for preventing its spread into the Territories; aimed to persuade voters by moral, legal, historical, economic, and rhetorical reasoning. The text models how to structure arguments, rebut opponents, and appeal to public duty and founding principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the full magnitude of the issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not underestimate the size of the question; 'small cures for great sores--plasters too small to cover the wound' will produce only temporary settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the scale and persistence of the problem (e.g., repeated attempts to 'settle' slavery failed). Use quantitative or vivid statements (here: 'one sixth of the whole population... are slaves') to show scope. Anti-pattern: offering half-measures or trivial compromises that fail to address root causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a clear philosophical basis for policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Any lasting policy must 'rest upon some philosophical opinion.' There are essentially two consistent bases: (a) slavery is right (property view) or (b) slavery is wrong; policies must follow coherently from whichever basis is chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the underlying moral/philosophical position and derive policy consistently from it. Scoring note: policies presented without an articulated philosophical foundation are unstable and likely to fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the issue morally and politically: declare slavery wrong where votes reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Assert that slavery is a 'great moral, social, and political evil' and argue one should 'treat it as a wrong in the Territories, where our votes will reach it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use moral language to justify political action where legal authority exists (e.g., Territories). Anti-pattern: refusing to call the practice wrong publicly or politically, which undermines moral clarity and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refute and expose the 'indifference' or middle-ground stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the policy of 'popular sovereignty' or 'I don't care whether it be voted up or down' as implausible and baseless; show that public indifference cannot be sustained and would nationalize slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate internal contradictions and long-term consequences of professed indifference. Use hypothetical public-opinion shifts and their outcomes to show why middle-ground positions are unsustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain opponents' motives via material interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute opponents' views in part to pecuniary interest: owners see slaves as property; 'this two thousand millions of dollars ... has its influence upon their minds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economic explanation to account for cognitive bias and resistance to moral argument. Example: show how concentrated monetary interest shapes legal and political positions; anti-pattern: treating opposition as purely ideological without acknowledging material incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid analogies and concrete imagery to make abstract dangers tangible
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ memorable metaphors (venomous snake in the road; snakes in the bed) to illustrate the risk of introducing slavery into new Territories: 'The new Territories are the newly made bed... whether they shall have snakes mixed up with them or not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose analogies that map clearly to the audience's experience and the stakes at issue. These make abstract policy consequences emotionally comprehensible and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to founding fathers and constitutional practice as historical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Support positions by showing how 'our fathers, who framed this Government,' regarded slavery (e.g., prohibited the spread into Territories, suspended slave trade for 20 years). Use constitutional wording and historical acts as evidence they considered slavery wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific historical acts, framers' behavior, and constitutional phrasing (ambiguities around 'persons held to service') to argue continuity with founding principles. Anti-pattern: invoking Washington or the framers selectively without showing consistency of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose rhetorical tactics and demand proof for accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: Label dishonest opponent tactics (e.g., 'bushwhacking,' slander such as charging Republicans with John Brown's actions) and insist that accusations be supported by specific proof rather than repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rebutting charges, call for specific evidence or identify them as malicious if unsupported. This both defends reputation and undermines cheap political attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect moral positions to the audience's self-interest and labor concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Show how slavery affects free white labor and industry (e.g., shoe strike, competition with owned labor, degradation of local labor markets), arguing that preventing slavery's spread protects opportunities for free labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local economic examples to make the case that moral policy also has material benefits for the audience. Anti-pattern: treating moral arguments as abstract and detached from constituents' livelihoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge inconsistent professed beliefs by testing actions, not words
rubrics_metrics.description: Test those who claim slavery is wrong by their actions (e.g., support for emancipation movements); 'You say that you think slavery is wrong, but you denounce all attempts to restrain it. Is there anything else that you think wrong that you are not willing to deal with as wrong?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose hypocrisy by proposing concrete tests of commitment (voting, supporting emancipation parties). Reward actions over mere verbal assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate calmness, restraint, and principled conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when provoked, 'let us do nothing through passion and ill-temper' and seek to act 'calmly' and with duty toward harmony among states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model temperate rhetoric and counsel against inflammatory responses. This increases credibility and reduces charges of extremism; anti-pattern: responding to slander with equal or greater passion that alienates moderates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical contrasts to show mutually exclusive outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up clear either/or contrasts (e.g., if slavery is right then anti-slavery words/acts are wrong; if slavery is wrong then its extension must be resisted) to show the stakes and force consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the debate in terms that force opponents to reveal the logical implications of their positions; scoring note: arguments that expose contradictions are rhetorically strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground appeals to duty and faith in moral rightness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude appeals by asserting confidence that 'right makes might' and urging citizens to 'dare to do our duty as we understand it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End persuasive addresses with a call to conscience and duty to motivate sustained commitment. This ties moral rhetoric to political action and perseverance.
